newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Aborigines threaten trade action against Australia.
newsitem.headline: Aborigines threaten trade action against Australia.

text.p: Aboriginal leaders on Friday threatened to seek international trade sanctions against Australia over its treatment of native land rights.
"We've just about exhausted the process of diplomacy in this country with this particular government," Aboriginal leader Geoff Clark said after meeting Prime Minister John Howard.
"We have to seek some sort of remedy in the United Nations forums and I think that we need to be starting to be going around talking about trade sanctions against Australia."
The Liberal-National government's still to be announced native title policy is expected to limit native title after a 1996 High Court judgement allowed native title on pastoral land.
But Prime Minister John Howard is trying to develop a compromise to regulate native title, granted by the High Court in 1992, that will satisfy both farmers and Aborigines.
Howard has said that 78 percent of Australia's 7.68 million square km (2.96 sq miles) of land was "potentially claimable" by Aborigines under native title laws.
Farmers are demanding Aboriginal native title rights be extinguished to protect the rural industry, which they say is hamstrung by uncertainty until the government develops a policy.
Clark said Aborigines had proposed to Howard on Friday a compromise in which they would share the land, but they insist any deal must not include extinguishment of their rights.
Howard has said the row created by the High Court's 1996 Wik decision is the greatest problem facing his year-old conservative administration.

In its decision, Australia's highest court ruled long-term pastoral leases granted to farmers in the more than 200 years of European settlement to use government land did not automatically wipe out Aboriginal rights to use the land. But the court did not, however, spell out exactly what rights Aborigines now had.

Farmers say they cannot make business decisions until the government clarifies the issue with legislation. Some miners also operate on pastoral leases and the confusion has halted government processing of some exploration applications.
The former Labor government went through an even more protracted and bitter process of negotiation in 1993 in response to the High Court's original ruling on native title.
Former Labor prime minister Paul Keating eventually pushed native title laws through parliament, but the laws assumed that there was no native title on pastoral leases.
Last year the High Court unexpectedly declared that there was, reviving the issue.
Aborigines say that if they lose their native title rights it will reflect a totally loss of rights for indigenous people.
"It really indicates that Aboriginal people have got no rights under the legal system," said Clark.
